title: A Tutorial on Gumbel-Max Watermarking for Language Models

Uniform.short: $\U(0,1)$ denotes the continuous uniform distribution on the unit interval $(0,1)$.
Uniform.details: The continuous $\U(0,1)$ distribution has constant density $f(u)=1$ for $0<u<1$, so intervals of equal length have equal probability. Its CDF is $F(u)=u$ on $0\le u\le1$, its mean is $1/2$, and its variance is $1/12$. Strict and non-strict inequalities have the same probability because the distribution is continuous.

Exp.short: An exponential distribution is a continuous probability distribution on the nonnegative real numbers, controlled by a positive rate parameter $\lambda$.
Exp.details: With rate $\lambda>0$, its density is $f_Y(x)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$ and its survival function is $\Pr(Y>x)=e^{-\lambda x}$ for $x\ge0$. Its mean is $1/\lambda$, and it is memoryless: $\Pr(Y>s+t\mid Y>s)=\Pr(Y>t)$. The inverse-transform identity $-\log U\sim\Exp(1)$ holds for $U\sim\U(0,1)$, and if $E\sim\Exp(1)$ with $c>0$, then $E/c\sim\Exp(c)$.

Gumbel.short: A Gumbel distribution is a continuous probability distribution on the real line, often associated with random maxima.
Gumbel.details: The standard Gumbel distribution has CDF $\Pr(G\le g)=e^{-e^{-g}}$ for $g\in\mathbb R$ and density $f(g)=e^{-(g+e^{-g})}$. It belongs to the classical extreme-value family. Adding independent standard Gumbel noise to log-probabilities turns an argmax into an exact categorical sample (the Gumbel-max trick).

CDF.short: The cumulative distribution function (CDF) $F_X(x)=\Pr(X\le x)$ gives the probability that a random variable takes a value at most $x$.
CDF.details: For continuous variables the CDF is nondecreasing with limits $0$ and $1$; a smaller CDF at every threshold means a stochastically larger distribution. The survival function is $\Pr(X>x)=1-F_X(x)$.

Gamma.short: A Gamma distribution with shape $k>0$ and rate $\lambda>0$ is a continuous probability distribution on the nonnegative real numbers.
Gamma.details: Its density is $f(x)=\lambda^k x^{k-1}e^{-\lambda x}/\Gamma(k)$ for $x\ge0$, where $\Gamma(k)$ is the Gamma function. When $k$ is a positive integer, a sum of $k$ independent exponential variables with common rate $\lambda$ is Gamma distributed with shape $k$ and rate $\lambda$; its mean is $k/\lambda$ and its variance is $k/\lambda^2$.

GammaFunction.label: Gamma function
GammaFunction.short: The Gamma function $\Gamma(k)=\int_0^\infty t^{k-1}e^{-t}\,dt$ generalizes the factorial to positive non-integer arguments.
GammaFunction.details: For positive integer $k$, $\Gamma(k)=(k-1)!$. It appears as the normalizing constant of the Gamma distribution density, ensuring the density integrates to one.

Beta.short: A Beta distribution is a continuous probability distribution on the unit interval $(0,1)$ with two positive shape parameters.
Beta.details: This tutorial uses $\Beta(a,1)$, whose density is $f(x)=a x^{a-1}$ for $0<x<1$ and whose CDF is $F(x)=x^{a}$ on $0\le x\le1$. It arises here as the conditional distribution of a selected uniform value under watermarking.

PRF.short: A pseudorandom function ($\PRF$) is deterministic for a fixed key but designed to be computationally indistinguishable from a random function without that key.
PRF.details: The same key and inputs always produce the same output, so two parties holding the key can recompute identical values independently. Changing an input produces a new random-looking value, although finite outputs can collide.

argmax.short: $\argmax$ returns the argument at which an objective attains its maximum.
argmax.details: Applying a strictly increasing function to every objective value preserves its $\argmax$; negating the objective exchanges maximization and minimization.

exponential_race.short: An exponential race selects the minimum among several independent exponential variables.
exponential_race.details: For independent exponential variables with rates $\lambda_j$, $\Pr(X_i=\min_jX_j)=\lambda_i/\sum_j\lambda_j$. Exponential races are a standard construction for categorical sampling.

pivot.short: A statistical pivot is a statistic whose reference distribution does not depend on unknown nuisance parameters.
pivot.details: Pivots allow model-free null calibration of statistical tests because their reference distributions are known without estimating unknown quantities.

p_value.short: A p-value is the null-hypothesis probability of obtaining a test statistic at least as extreme as the observed one.
p_value.details: A valid p-value is calibrated under the null and depends on the pre-specified testing protocol; small values indicate evidence against the null.

annotations.label: this annotated phrase
annotations.short: This is an example of the short explanation shown when you hover over blue annotated text.
annotations.details: Clicking an authored IperPaper annotation opens this longer explanation in the side panel. Throughout the tutorial, annotations use the same interaction to explain a symbol, equation step, notation choice, or concept in its local context.

annotations.label: $\mathbf p_t=(p_{t,1},\ldots,p_{t,V})$
annotations.short: $\mathbf p_t$ is the language model's categorical distribution at token position $t$.
annotations.details: Its $i$th coordinate $p_{t,i}$ is the probability assigned to candidate token $i$; all coordinates are nonnegative and sum to one.

annotations.label: $\sum_{i=1}^{V}p_{t,i}=1$
annotations.short: The candidate probabilities sum to one.
annotations.details: $\sum_{i=1}^{V}p_{t,i}=1$ makes $\mathbf p_t$ a valid categorical distribution over the $V$ vocabulary entries.

annotations.label: $r_{t,i}\in(0,1)$
annotations.short: $r_{t,i}$ is the secret-key-derived value for candidate $i$ at position $t$.
annotations.details: The ideal analysis treats these values as independent $\U(0,1)$ variables. In the implementation described by Li et al., the key and preceding tokens determine a PCG-64 seed, and candidate index $i$ selects the $i$th entry of the regenerated vector. NumPy's floating-point generator returns values in $[0,1)$, so an implementation applying logarithms should explicitly avoid exact endpoints.

annotations.label: $w_t$
annotations.short: $w_t$ is the token index actually emitted at position $t$.
annotations.details: The Gumbel-max decoder chooses $w_t$ by ranking every supported candidate with its model probability and keyed pseudorandom value.

annotations.label: $r_{t,w_t}$
annotations.short: $r_{t,w_t}$ is the keyed value attached to the token that was actually emitted.
annotations.details: It is the $i=w_t$ coordinate of the candidate vector $(r_{t,1},\ldots,r_{t,V})$. The verifier regenerates this chosen coordinate and uses it as the detection pivot.

annotations.label: $\PRF_{\Key}(w_{t-m},\ldots,w_{t-1},i)$
annotations.short: $\PRF_{\Key}$ is a pseudorandom function that takes the secret key, the preceding token context, and candidate-token index $i$, and produces a deterministic value $r_{t,i}$ in $(0,1)$ that appears random to someone without the key.
annotations.details: The same key, context, and candidate index always produce the same value, allowing the generator and verifier to compute $r_{t,i}$ independently. Changing an input is intended to produce a new random-looking value, although finite hash or pseudorandom outputs can collide. In the implementation described by Li et al., the key and preceding $m$ tokens determine a PCG-64 seed, and $i$ selects the corresponding entry of the generated candidate vector. Both parties must use the same key, tokenization, context rule, hashing method, pseudorandom generator, and candidate ordering.

annotations.label: $\argmax_{i:p_{t,i}>0}$
annotations.short: This $\argmax$ searches the supported candidates $i$ with $p_{t,i}>0$.
annotations.details: It returns the index whose keyed score $r_{t,i}^{1/p_{t,i}}$ is largest; zero-probability candidates are excluded because they cannot be emitted.

annotations.label: $r_{t,i}^{1/p_{t,i}}$
annotations.short: $r_{t,i}^{1/p_{t,i}}$ combines candidate $i$'s model probability $p_{t,i}$ with its keyed pseudorandom value $r_{t,i}$. The generator emits the candidate with the largest such score.
annotations.details: Because $0<r_{t,i}<1$, a larger keyed value gives a larger score. A larger model probability makes the exponent $1/p_{t,i}$ smaller, which keeps the score closer to one and therefore also favors that candidate. Thus the rule balances model preference with secret pseudorandomness. Although the score itself is not a probability, maximizing it selects candidate $i$ with probability exactly $p_{t,i}$ when the keyed values behave as independent uniforms. This is equivalent to minimizing $(-\log r_{t,i})/p_{t,i}$.

annotations.label: $\argmax_{i:p_{t,i}>0}r_{t,i}^{1/p_{t,i}}$
annotations.short: This first line substitutes the power-form selection rule from Equation (1).
annotations.details: By definition, $w_t$ is the supported candidate $i$ maximizing $r_{t,i}^{1/p_{t,i}}$. The condition $p_{t,i}>0$ keeps the exponent finite and excludes candidates that the model cannot emit.

annotations.label: $\argmax_{i:p_{t,i}>0}\log(r_{t,i}^{1/p_{t,i}})$
annotations.short: Applying $\log$ does not change the $\argmax$ because every score is positive and $\log$ is strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$.
annotations.details: For any two candidates, $r_{t,i}^{1/p_{t,i}} \ge r_{t,j}^{1/p_{t,j}}$ if and only if their logarithms have the same ordering. Strict monotonicity also preserves ties, so the entire maximizing set is unchanged.

annotations.label: $\argmax_{i:p_{t,i}>0}\frac{1}{p_{t,i}}\log r_{t,i}$
annotations.short: The identity $\log(x^a)=a\log x$ gives $\log(r_{t,i}^{1/p_{t,i}})=(1/p_{t,i})\log r_{t,i}$.
annotations.details: Here $r_{t,i}>0$, so its logarithm is defined, and $p_{t,i}>0$, so the real exponent $1/p_{t,i}$ is finite. The equality is applied separately to every candidate score inside the same $\argmax$.

annotations.label: $\argmax_{i:p_{t,i}>0}\frac{\log r_{t,i}}{p_{t,i}}$
annotations.short: The factor $(1/p_{t,i})\log r_{t,i}$ is algebraically the same as $\log r_{t,i}/p_{t,i}$.
annotations.details: This line only rewrites multiplication by the reciprocal: $a(1/b)=a/b$ for $b\ne0$. The candidate set already requires $p_{t,i}>0$, so division by $p_{t,i}$ is valid.

annotations.label: $\argmin_{i:p_{t,i}>0}\frac{-\log r_{t,i}}{p_{t,i}}$
annotations.short: Multiplying every objective value by $-1$ reverses its ordering, so maximizing $\log r_{t,i}/p_{t,i}$ is equivalent to minimizing $-\log r_{t,i}/p_{t,i}$.
annotations.details: If $f_i\ge f_j$, then $-f_i\le-f_j$; therefore $\argmax_i f_i=\argmin_i(-f_i)$, including the same tie set. The next proof interprets the resulting auxiliary variable using the standard exponential-race analogy.

annotations.label: $\Pr(w_t=i\mid\mathbf p_t)=p_{t,i}$
annotations.short: Conditioned on $\mathbf p_t$, candidate $i$ is emitted with probability $p_{t,i}$.
annotations.details: Averaging over the hidden pseudorandomness recovers the language model's intended next-token distribution exactly. The watermark changes the coupling, not this marginal.

annotations.label: Gumbel distribution
annotations.short: A Gumbel distribution is a continuous probability distribution on the real line, often associated with random maxima.
annotations.details: This tutorial uses the standard Gumbel distribution with CDF $\Pr(G\le g)=e^{-e^{-g}}$. One independent Gumbel noise value is assigned to each candidate so that adding the noise to $\log p_{t,i}$ turns an argmax into an exact categorical sample.

annotations.label: Gumbel-max sampler
annotations.short: The Gumbel-max sampler draws from categorical probabilities by adding independent standard Gumbel noise to each log-probability and taking the largest score.
annotations.details: For candidate probabilities $p_{t,i}$, it returns $\argmax_i(\log p_{t,i}+G_{t,i})$, where the $G_{t,i}$ are independent standard Gumbel variables. Candidate $i$ wins with probability exactly $p_{t,i}$; in this watermark, keyed uniform values generate reproducible Gumbel noise.

annotations.label: $G_{t,i}=-\log(-\log r_{t,i})$
annotations.short: $G_{t,i}=-\log(-\log r_{t,i})$ transforms a uniform value into standard Gumbel noise.
annotations.details: Its cumulative distribution is $\Pr(G_{t,i}\le g)=e^{-e^{-g}}$. Adding it to $\log p_{t,i}$ gives the classical additive Gumbel-max rule.

annotations.label: $X_{t,i}$
annotations.short: $X_{t,i}:=(-\log r_{t,i})/p_{t,i}$ is an auxiliary score used to express token selection as a minimization.
annotations.details: When $r_{t,i}$ behaves as a uniform random value, $X_{t,i}$ has an exponential distribution with rate $p_{t,i}$. The generator selects the candidate with the smallest $X_{t,i}$; this minimum construction is known as an exponential race.

annotations.label: $-\log r_{t,i}\sim\Exp(\text{rate}=1)$
annotations.short: Taking the negative logarithm of $r_{t,i}\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)$ produces an exponential variable with rate $1$.
annotations.details: The proof computes the survival function: for $x\ge0$, $\Pr(-\log r_{t,i}>x)=\Pr(r_{t,i}<e^{-x})=e^{-x}$. This matches $\mathrm{Exp}(\text{rate}=1)$.

annotations.label: exponential distribution
annotations.short: An exponential distribution is a continuous probability distribution on the nonnegative real numbers, controlled by a positive rate parameter.
annotations.details: With rate $\lambda>0$, its density is $f_Y(x)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$ and its survival function is $\Pr(Y>x)=e^{-\lambda x}$ for $x\ge0$. Its mean is $1/\lambda$.

annotations.label: $f_Y(x)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x},\quad \Pr(Y>x)=e^{-\lambda x}$
annotations.short: These are the density and survival function of an exponential variable with rate $\lambda$.
annotations.details: The survival function is the probability of exceeding $x$. Integrating the density from $x$ to infinity gives $\int_x^\infty \lambda e^{-\lambda u}\,du=e^{-\lambda x}$.

annotations.label: $Y_{t,i}:=-\log r_{t,i}$
annotations.short: $Y_{t,i}$ abbreviates the transformed uniform value $-\log r_{t,i}$.
annotations.details: Because $r_{t,i}\in(0,1)$, its logarithm is negative and $Y_{t,i}\ge0$, matching the support of an exponential distribution.

annotations.label: $\Pr(-\log r_{t,i}>x)$
annotations.short: Substitute the definition $Y_{t,i}=-\log r_{t,i}$ into the tail event $Y_{t,i}>x$.
annotations.details: This changes only the notation inside the probability; it does not alter the event or its probability.

annotations.label: $\Pr(\log r_{t,i}<-x)$
annotations.short: Multiplying $-\log r_{t,i}>x$ by $-1$ reverses the inequality, giving $\log r_{t,i}<-x$.
annotations.details: For real numbers, multiplying both sides of an inequality by a negative value reverses its direction.

annotations.label: $\Pr(r_{t,i}<e^{-x})$
annotations.short: Exponentiating preserves the inequality because $e^z$ is strictly increasing.
annotations.details: The event $\log r_{t,i}<-x$ is equivalent to $e^{\log r_{t,i}}<e^{-x}$, and $e^{\log r_{t,i}}=r_{t,i}$ because $r_{t,i}>0$.

annotations.label: $e^{-x}$
annotations.short: Since $r_{t,i}$ is uniform on $(0,1)$, $\Pr(r_{t,i}<u)=u$ for $0\le u\le1$.
annotations.details: For $x\ge0$, the threshold $u=e^{-x}$ lies in $(0,1]$, so $\Pr(r_{t,i}<e^{-x})=e^{-x}$. Strict and non-strict inequalities have the same probability because the uniform distribution is continuous.

annotations.label: $X_{t,i}\sim\Exp(\text{rate}=p_{t,i})$
annotations.short: $X_{t,i}$ is exponential with rate $p_{t,i}$.
annotations.details: Because $-\log r_{t,i}\sim\Exp(1)$, division by $p_{t,i}$ changes the rate to $p_{t,i}$ and the mean to $1/p_{t,i}$.

annotations.label: $\Pr(X_{t,i}=\min_jX_{t,j})=p_{t,i}$
annotations.short: Candidate $i$ has the smallest auxiliary value $X_{t,i}$ with probability $p_{t,i}$.
annotations.details: For independent exponential variables, the probability that variable $i$ is the minimum equals its rate divided by the sum of all rates. Here the rates are $p_{t,i}$ and $\sum_jp_{t,j}=1$, so the probability is exactly $p_{t,i}$.

annotations.label: exponential race
annotations.short: An exponential race selects the minimum among several independent exponential variables.
annotations.details: Assigning candidate $i$ the exponential rate $p_{t,i}$ makes its probability of attaining the minimum equal to the desired categorical probability $p_{t,i}$.

annotations.label: $H_0$
annotations.short: $H_0$ says the observed text is independent of this secret watermark randomness.
annotations.details: It includes human text and ordinary unwatermarked model output when their token choices are independent of the tested keyed pseudorandom field. Lack of access to the key is normally sufficient in the ideal model, but does not by itself rule out correlations inherited from copied or watermarked context.

annotations.label: $H_1$
annotations.short: $H_1$ says the text was generated by the keyed Gumbel-max watermark.
annotations.details: Under this alternative, selected token indices are positively coupled to the secret pseudorandom field.

annotations.label: $r_{t,w_t}\sim\mathrm U(0,1)$
annotations.short: Under $H_0$, the selected keyed value is uniform on $(0,1)$.
annotations.details: The observed token is independent of the secret field under the ideal null, so selecting coordinate $w_t$ does not bias $r_{t,w_t}$.

annotations.label: $\Pr_1(r_{t,w_t}\le x\mid\mathbf p_t)=\sum_i p_{t,i}x^{1/p_{t,i}}$
annotations.short: This is the conditional CDF of the selected keyed value under watermarking.
annotations.details: The mixture $\sum_i p_{t,i}x^{1/p_{t,i}}$ lies below the uniform CDF $x$ on $(0,1)$, so $r_{t,w_t}$ is stochastically shifted toward one.

annotations.label: $Z_t=-\log(1-r_{t,w_t})$
annotations.short: $Z_t=-\log(1-r_{t,w_t})$ converts a selected value near one into a large positive score.
annotations.details: Under the ideal null, $Z_t\sim\Exp(1)$; watermarking tends to increase it because the selected $r_{t,w_t}$ is biased upward.

annotations.label: $S_T=\sum_{t=1}^{T}-\log(1-r_{t,w_t})$
annotations.short: $S_T$ sums the per-token evidence over $T$ scored positions.
annotations.details: Large values favor the watermarked alternative. Its simple Gamma calibration requires the effective scored positions to be independent under $H_0$.

annotations.label: $S_T\sim\Gam(\text{shape}=T,\text{rate}=1)$
annotations.short: Under independent effective positions, $S_T$ has a Gamma distribution with shape $T$ and rate one.
annotations.details: It is the sum of $T$ independent $\Exp(1)$ scores, so its null mean and variance are both $T$. Repeated-context or pseudorandom collisions can violate this independence, in which case the simple Gamma calibration need not apply.

annotations.label: one-sided p-value
annotations.short: The p-value is the null probability of obtaining a score at least as large as the observed one.
annotations.details: Here it is $\Pr_{H_0}(S_T\ge S_T^{\rm obs})$ because unusually large scores are evidence for watermarking.

annotations.label: pivot
annotations.short: The selected value is a pivot because its null distribution is known without the unknown model probabilities.
annotations.details: Under text independent of the tested keyed pseudorandom field, $r_{t,w_t}\sim\U(0,1)$ regardless of $\mathbf p_t$, enabling model-free null calibration for chosen-coordinate detectors.
